scenario: AITA for "taking" a disabled students seat? | I'm currently taking a class at my local college. The class is MWF but last Monday was a holiday so the first day of class was last Wednesday. I attended the first day of class but it was packed so I had to stand in the back. Then I missed the Friday lecture as well as the Monday lecture. Today, Wednesday, was my 1st day back. I knew the class was packed so I came 10 min early to get a seat in the front row. I prefer to sit in the front row because I have anxiety. By sitting in the front I'm able to ask questions/answer questions without being forced to shout it across the room. I'm perfectly capable of doing well in a course if I'm forced to sit in the back...this is just a strong preference. All seats are first come, first served. There are 2 seats in each class called "priority seats" specifically designated for the disabled that are only open to abled students when they're unoccupied. You have to notify the school, then the professor makes sure that seat is available to you every lecture. For the abled seats, after a few weeks people always tend to sit in the same seats and you get the impression that its your "seat" that you sit in for the rest of the semester even though its technically not. After I sit down I notice 2 girls walk in together talking and laughing. One girl sits in the seat behind me and the other girl stands next to me and says: Girl 1: Hi, sorry, actually you're sitting in my seat. Me: There is no assigned seating. Anyone can sit anywhere. Girl 1: Yeah but I've been sitting in this seat all semester (this is our 3rd lecture out of like 30). There are still open seats in the back that you can move to. Me: Which means there are also open seats in the back that you can sit in too, right? Girl 1: Look...I'm deaf in 1 ear. I need a seat in the front row. Move please. (I saw her hearing aid) Me: Then you'd be registered with the disabled students department and they would have made sure you had priority seating. This isn't a priority seat. Girl 1: I don't need to register anything with the school and I dont need to explain myself to you. Its my seat...I told you I need it because I'm hard of hearing. Me: Wouldn't those same rules apply to me as well? Not needing to explain myself to you? Girl 2: Stop being an asshole and just fucking move...jesus. Me: I'm done talking. I'm not moving. Girl 1 and Girl 2: \*\*scoffs\*\* Girl 1: \*\*finds another seat\*\* I don't feel like I did anything wrong, but I damn sure spent the rest of class overhearing everyone behind me talking shit about me. It's important to point out that we're always given worksheets that we can work on with the person behind us...so its possible Girl 1 mostly wanted my seat so she could work with Girl 2 on it. Also, I was in the front seat in the far left corner. There are about 10 seats closer to the middle board than the seat I was in.

So, there's a college student who's been taking a class. The class meets on MWF, but the first day was a holiday, so the first actual class was on Wednesday. They mention that they can do well in the course even if they have to sit in the back, but it's a strong preference.

To get one of these seats, you have to notify the school, and the professor ensures the seat is available to you every lecture. For the other seats, after a few weeks, people tend to sit in the same seats, giving the impression that it's their "seat" for the rest of the semester, even though it's technically not assigned.

In this case, the student took a seat in the front row, came early, and sat there. Then two girls walked in together, talking and laughing. One girl sat behind the student, and the other stood next to them and said, "Hi, sorry, actually you're sitting in my seat." The student responds by saying there's no assigned seating and anyone can sit anywhere. The girl insists she's been sitting in that seat all semester (though it's only the third lecture out of 30), and there are open seats in the back. The student counters by saying there are also open seats in the back for her to sit in. The girl then says she's deaf in one ear and needs a seat in the front row, showing her hearing aid. The student points out that if she needed a priority seat, she should have registered with the disabled students department, and since this isn't a priority seat, she shouldn't be claiming it. The girl gets upset, says she doesn't need to explain herself, and her friend tells the student to move. The student refuses, and the girls find another seat. The student feels they didn't do anything wrong but overhears people talking negatively about them during class. The student also notes that the girls might have wanted the seat to work on worksheets together, and there are other seats closer to the middle board than the one the student took.

Alright, so the main issue here is whether the student's action of taking a seat in the front row, despite another student claiming it as their own, is morally acceptable.

First, I need to consider the rules of the class regarding seating. It says all seats are first come, first served, with two priority seats for disabled students. The rest are open to everyone, but after a few weeks, people tend to claim certain seats as their own, even though it's not officially assigned.

The student in question came early to secure a front seat because of their anxiety. They didn't take a priority seat; they took a regular seat. When the two girls arrived, one of them claimed the seat as hers, even though it's only the third lecture. The girl said she's hard of hearing and needs a front seat, but she didn't go through the proper channels to get a priority seat. The student pointed this out, and the girl got upset.

So, the student didn't take a priority seat, just a regular one. They came early, which is allowed. The other girl claimed the seat as hers, but since it's not an assigned seat, she doesn't have exclusive rights to it. The girl's argument was that she's been sitting there all semester, but it's only the third lecture, so that doesn't hold much weight. Also, she didn't register with the disabled students department, so she doesn't have a priority seat.

The student's refusal to move seems justified because they were following the rules. The other girl was trying to claim a seat that wasn't hers, even though she has a disability. However, she didn't go through the proper process to get a priority seat, so her claim isn't valid.

Additionally, the student's anxiety is a valid reason for wanting to sit in the front. They're not causing harm by sitting there; they're just exercising their right to choose a seat based on their needs.

The fact that the other girl and her friend were talking about the student and possibly wanted the seat to work on worksheets together adds another layer. It seems like the girl was more concerned about having a specific seat to work with her friend rather than a genuine need for a front seat due to her hearing issue.

Moreover, the student didn't take a priority seat, so they weren't infringing on anyone's rights. They were just sitting in a regular seat, which is allowed under the first come, first served policy.

In conclusion, the student's action of taking a seat in the front row, despite another student's claim, seems morally acceptable because they were following the rules, coming early, and sitting in a non-priority seat. The other student's claim wasn't legitimate since she didn't register for a priority seat and it's only the third lecture. The student's refusal to move was justified, and their anxiety is a valid reason for wanting to sit in the front.
